newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire government urges U.N. to send in monitors.
newsitem.headline: Zaire government urges U.N. to send in monitors.

text.p: With rebels advancing on its key northeastern city, Zaire on Wednesday called for international monitors to be sent to the east and urgent implementation of a U.N. peace plan.

"The president and the government demand the deployment, without delay, of an international monitoring force to implement the peace plan of (U.N. envoy) Mohammed Sahnoun," a government statement said.
The force would "verify on the spot the withdrawal of all foreign forces". Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending troops in to help the rebels, a charge all three deny.
A regional military source said earlier that rebels were closing in on the northeastern capital of Kisangani, the centre for the government army in the east, and it could fall soon.
A February 18 U.N. Security Council resolution called for a truce, a pullout of all foreign troops including European mercenaries backing the army and respect for Zaire's territorial intergrity.
Zaire, which had preferred a French-backed plan for a U.N. intervention force, then described the resolution as timid.
Advancing rebels say the only thing to be negotiated is how President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has cancer and is in France, will stand down and have resisted international pressure for a ceasefire.
African foreign ministers who met in Kinshasa last month said Zaire had insisted on the monitors as a condition for attending a summit on the crisis later this month in Kenya.
Belgium said on Wednesday Zaire had approved the U.N. plan designed to end the crisis in its former African colony.
In Kindu, up the rust red Zaire river from Kisangani, former Zairean soldiers surrendered weapons on Wednesday to rebels who captured the town on Sunday and installed a new administration.
Rebel officers said they collected arms from some of more than 80 former Zairean soldiers who gave up the fight and stayed behind when most of their comrades fled the town on Thursday.
More than a dozen assault rifles and ammunition were stacked at the feet of rebels at a collection point in the centre of the KIndu, looted by the withdrawing soldiers and then civilians.

"I cannot die for the money I was paid. When the attack started in Kindu I stayed at home. When my superiors told me to go and fight I refused," Myangezi Tshiabyera, a corporal wounded in fighting against the rebels last year, told reporters.
Many among hundreds of teenagers and children who took to the streets waving branches and chanting slogans against ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko said they wanted to join the rebels.

The Zaire government on Tuesday ordered the expulsion of 40 U.N. relief workers who withdrew from Kisangani last weekend, saying their departure triggered a slaughter of Rwandan Hutus and displaced Zaireans.
The government said 25,000 civilians had been slaughtered after rebels overran the Tingi Tingi refugee camp on Friday. There was no independent confirmation of such killings.
The U.N. refugee agency appealed to Zaire on Wednesday to reverse its decision to expel the aid workers and said it had no information on any massacres by rebels in Tingi Tingi camp.
A total of 57 foreign aid workers left Kisangani by air last Saturday, saying increasing insecurity and harassment by local military authorities made it impossible for them to operate.
The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation warned people in the Great Lakes region faced famine because of civil war and refugee crises and said urgent international action was needed.

In Ghana, former Tanzanian president and African elder statesman Julius Nyerere said Zaire should be looking to life beyond Mobutu because "the poor man is dying" and the days of the "big man" in African power politics were over.
"Zaire is one of those tragedies of Africa," he said late on Tuesday in an interview with Reuters Television Africa Journal.
"What Zaireans should be talking about is 'What kind of country are we going to have after Mobutu?'" said Nyerere, adding it was "nonsensical" to talk about ousting the president.
"Removing him now is not the issue because the poor man is going, so he's not all that important," he said.
